passage: During the free period in Class 9C, phones were meant to be in bags, but half the room was hunched over the class chat. Elizabeth scrolled. Someone had posted a photo of Anjali's lunch box with a cruel caption, and forty messages later people were calling Anjali names. Across the room Anjali sat perfectly straight, staring at her desk, her ears red. Elizabeth's thumb hovered over the keyboard. What if they turned on her next? Her stomach churned and she typed nothing. All afternoon her guilt weighed like a wet blanket. On the bus she opened a private chat and wrote, "I saw what they wrote. I'm sorry I said nothing. It was wrong and I'm on your side." Then the next morning she walked to Mr Fernandes and showed him the screenshots.

qa.q: What did someone post about Anjali's lunch box in the class chat?
qa.a: Someone posted a photo of Anjali's lunch box with a cruel caption.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when her thumb hovered over the keyboard?
qa.a: Scared and guilty. She worried that the group might turn on her next, and she felt her guilt weighed like a wet blanket all afternoon.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth do that helped more than staying quiet?
qa.a: She sent Anjali a private message saying she was on her side, and then showed Mr Fernandes the screenshots.

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt reading Elizabeth's private message?
qa.a: Probably relieved and less alone. She had sat rigid and red-eared while the chat piled on, so hearing someone was on her side may have meant a lot. 🤍

grounding: Elizabeth watches a classmate torn apart in the chat and stays silent, feeling guilty and scared, then sends a private message and reports to a teacher.

passage: The rumour was that I cheated in the unit test. I'm Varun, and I hadn't. Someone started it in a group chat, and by the next morning people were whispering as I walked in. My first instinct was to shout at the whole class. My second was to stay home forever. My chest was tight, and I couldn't eat breakfast. But I sat on the stairs and told myself to breathe. I didn't start a rumour back, though I could think of a few. I told my mother that evening and she came to school with me. I showed my teacher my rough work and the marks list, and posted once in the class chat, "I didn't cheat. My rough work is with the teacher." Nitin sat next to me at lunch the whole week. That helped more than any argument.

qa.q: What was the rumour about Varun?
qa.a: The rumour was that he cheated in the unit test.

qa.q: What were Varun's two first instincts, and how did he feel?
qa.a: He wanted to shout at the whole class or stay home forever, and he felt afraid, since his chest was tight and he couldn't eat breakfast.

qa.q: What did Varun do that helped him handle it?
qa.a: He calmed himself, told his mother, showed his teacher his rough work and the marks list, corrected it once in the chat and did not spread a rumour back.

qa.q: How might Nitin's choice to sit with Varun have felt to Varun?
qa.a: Like real support. Having someone next to him all week showed Varun the rumour had not turned everyone against him. 😊

grounding: A false rumour spreads about Varun; he stays calm, tells his mother and teacher, corrects it once with facts and leans on a real friend.

passage:
Dear Mrs Bhatt,

I'm writing because I can't say this out loud without crying. For about six weeks, Kamal has blocked me in the corridor outside the science lab and pushed my bag off my shoulder. He calls me names and the others laugh. I have told my mother I have a stomach ache four times so I don't have to come to school, but it isn't true. I feel sick when the bell rings. I used to think I must have done something to deserve it. I've started to believe that isn't true. I wrote down the dates: 3, 10 and 17 September, and yesterday. I stay near Anaya and Meher at break, and they don't laugh. Please can we talk after class on Monday? I'd rather not do this alone.

Arohi

qa.q: For about how long has Kamal been blocking Arohi in the corridor?
qa.a: He has been doing it for about six weeks.

qa.q: What is Arohi feeling about school, and how do you know?
qa.a: Dread and fear. She says she feels sick when the bell rings and has claimed stomach aches four times to avoid coming.

qa.q: What steps has Arohi taken that a wise person would suggest?
qa.a: She wrote down the dates, stays near supportive friends at break and is asking her teacher for a talk instead of facing it alone.

qa.q: How might Mrs Bhatt feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Probably concerned and glad Arohi trusted her. She now knows dates and details she can act on with the school.

grounding: Arohi dreads the corridor and lies about being sick because of a bully, and writes to a trusted teacher with dates, staying near supportive friends.

passage: Ujjwal's fists were clenched under the desk. Kishore had grabbed his tiffin again at recess and thrown it in the bin, and the whole back row snorted. That night Ujjwal lay awake seeing Kishore's smirk and imagining, in scary detail, making him feel every second of it. The pictures were so vivid they frightened him. He realised his hatred was as big as the hurt behind it. He didn't want to become someone who does that to another person, or end up in trouble himself. In the morning he told his older sister Radhika everything, his voice cracking. She didn't tell him he was overreacting. "This is not something you should carry alone," she said. "Let's go and see the vice principal together." Ujjwal nodded, and his fists finally opened.

qa.q: What did Kishore do with Ujjwal's tiffin at recess?
qa.a: He grabbed it and threw it in the bin.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal realise about the pictures in his head?
qa.a: He realised his hatred was as big as the hurt behind it, and that it frightened him because he did not want to become someone who does that to another person.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do that was wise?
qa.a: He told his sister Radhika, shared the anger with her and agreed to go to the vice principal together instead of retaliating.

qa.q: How might Radhika see Ujjwal's anger?
qa.a: As a sign that he has been badly hurt, not as overreacting. She takes it seriously and suggests adult help.

grounding: Ujjwal hates the boy who torments him and pictures hurting him, but shares it with his sister and seeks adult intervention instead of retaliating.

passage:
Day 1. At recess Francis mimicked Ankita's stammer and the boys roared. He felt ten feet tall, until Ankita's eyes went shiny and he noticed his own laugh sounded thin.

Day 3. At home his father shouted about the electricity bill, then about Francis's marks, then about nothing. Francis stayed in his room, smaller than he had felt all day. The next morning he shoved a Class 8 boy's books off a bench and everybody laughed again. The strong feeling lasted about a minute.

Day 10. His class teacher asked him to stay back. "You seem angry lately. Is something happening?" Francis stared at his shoes and said, "Home isn't good." The teacher walked him to the counsellor. He didn't feel strong, but he felt less alone.

qa.q: What did Francis mimic at recess on Day 1?
qa.a: He mimicked Ankita's stammer.

qa.q: What might Francis be covering with the bullying, and what shows it?
qa.a: Hurt at home. After his father's shouting he feels smaller than all day and shoves a boy's books the next morning, while the feeling of strength lasts only about a minute.

qa.q: What helped Francis on Day 10?
qa.a: His teacher asked kindly, Francis said home was not good, and the teacher took him to the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt when Francis mimicked her?
qa.a: Humiliated and hurt. Her eyes went shiny while the boys roared.

grounding: Francis bullies because it feels strong while hiding hurt at home, and eventually a teacher and counsellor help.

passage:
Sharmila to Aarav (brother)
Sharmila: Minakshi is such a nobody. She trips over her own bag lol
Sharmila: honestly she's fair game, everyone knows it
Aarav: why does she bother you so much
Sharmila: she doesn't. She's just weak
Aarav: then why do you keep talking about her
Sharmila: ...
Sharmila: because she cried in class and I felt sick
Aarav: sick like guilty?
Sharmila: sick like scared
Sharmila: if she can be that weak then maybe I could be too
Aarav: that's a lot to notice
Sharmila: I know. I was picked last for hockey last week and I laughed it off. I think I've been making her the weak one so it isn't me

qa.q: What did Sharmila say Minakshi trips over?
qa.a: She said Minakshi trips over her own bag.

qa.q: What does Sharmila realise she is afraid of?
qa.a: She realises she is scared of being weak herself. Seeing Minakshi cry made her feel sick because it could have been her.

qa.q: What could Sharmila do next after this realisation?
qa.a: She could stop treating Minakshi as fair game, notice when the old story shows up, and keep talking with Aarav about the fear, and not turn contempt into a public habit.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel when she is talked about this way?
qa.a: Small and picked on, and afraid to come to school, since being called a nobody and cried over in class hurt her.

grounding: Sharmila looks down on a weaker classmate and treats her as fair game, then recognises the contempt covers her own fear of being weak.

passage: Looking back, I can still see it. Irawati was standing at the front of the class while three boys imitated her walk, and half the room was laughing. I laughed too, just once, a small breath through my nose, before I felt sick. Nobody said a word. I stayed in my seat and pretended to look for my pencil. All day I kept replaying it, ashamed that I'd done nothing, ashamed that I'd laughed. That evening I decided it mattered even if it was small. I sent Irawati a note in her locker: "That was not okay. I'm sorry I laughed. I'm here if you want to talk." The next day I told the class teacher what happened. Since then, when I hear that kind of joke, I don't laugh. I'm Sarika, and it isn't much, but it's mine to do.

qa.q: Where was Irawati standing when the boys imitated her walk?
qa.a: She was standing at the front of the class.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling after the incident?
qa.a: Ashamed. She kept replaying it and felt bad both that she did nothing and that she had laughed once.

qa.q: What small steps did Sarika take?
qa.a: She left Irawati a kind note in her locker, told the class teacher the next day and decided not to laugh at that kind of joke again.

qa.q: How might Irawati have felt reading Sarika's note?
qa.a: Probably relieved and less alone, because someone who had been in the room said it was not okay.

grounding: Sarika saw a classmate bullied, did nothing and felt ashamed, then checked on her privately, reported to a teacher and refused to laugh.

passage:
Dear Tejas,

You probably noticed I was shaking yesterday at the water cooler. My knees were like jelly when those boys took your notebook and held it over your head. I didn't shout, and I didn't try to grab it. I just stood next to you and said, "Give it back. I'm going to get Sir." I don't know why it worked, but Rohan dropped it and they walked away. I was scared they'd come for me next. I went straight to Mr Desai and told him what I saw, and he said he'd speak to them. I don't want you to feel embarrassed or think I felt sorry for you. Anyone could have been in your place. If it happens again, I'll stand by you again, and we'll go to Sir together.

Vinita

qa.q: What did the boys do with Tejas's notebook?
qa.a: They took it and held it over his head.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel when she stood beside Tejas?
qa.a: Frightened but steady. Her knees were like jelly and she worried they would come for her next, yet she stayed calm and spoke.

qa.q: What did Vinita do that was wise?
qa.a: She stayed calm, stood beside Tejas, did not fight and went to Mr Desai straight away.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel when he reads the letter?
qa.a: Probably relieved and grateful, and perhaps a little embarrassed. Vinita says that anyone could have been in his place, so he does not feel pitied.

grounding: Vinita stands up for a classmate being bullied by staying calm, standing beside him and getting an adult early instead of fighting.

passage: Thursday night. I feel sick and I don't know why I still feel safe. Gopika gave me the window seat today and shared her chips because I laughed when she called Meera a name. Everyone else laughed, and Gopika smiled at me like I'd passed a test. I felt warm for about ten seconds, and then I saw Meera's face and my stomach dropped. I don't even dislike Meera. I just don't want to be the person Gopika picks next. But being safe shouldn't depend on hurting someone. Tomorrow I'm going to sit with Nisha and the library kids. Gopika will probably be cold to me, or worse. I'm scared of that. I'll speak to Ma'am if it gets bad. And I'm going to say sorry to Meera. — Sangeeta

qa.q: What did Gopika give Sangeeta after she laughed?
qa.a: She gave Sangeeta the window seat and shared her chips.

qa.q: What mixed feelings does Sangeeta describe?
qa.a: Feeling safe and sick together. She felt warm for ten seconds after being rewarded, then her stomach dropped when she saw Meera's face.

qa.q: What plan does Sangeeta make?
qa.a: She will sit with Nisha and the library kids, tell Ma'am if it gets bad and apologise to Meera, so she no longer takes part.

qa.q: How might Meera have felt when she saw the others laughing?
qa.a: Hurt and alone, since she was the one called a name while everyone laughed.

grounding: A bully rewards Sangeeta for joining in; she feels safe and sick, and writes that she will step away even at some risk.

passage: The bus was leaving in ten minutes and the whole school was crowded into the porch, shouting over the monsoon rain. Harish stood by the wall, his bag pressed to his chest, trying to disappear. Ojas had been taking his lunch money for weeks. Today Ojas grabbed the strap of Harish's bag and hissed, "Hand it over." Then Mr Desai appeared through the crowd with an umbrella. "Ojas, come with me. Harish, wait here with me for a moment." Harish's knees almost gave way, from relief and from a hot flush of embarrassment that everyone had seen. "I'm not going to make you say everything now," the teacher said quietly, "but I need the dates you remember." Harish took a shaky breath and told him. The bus horn honked, and for the first time in weeks he wasn't dreading the ride home.

qa.q: Why was the porch crowded at the end of the day?
qa.a: The bus was leaving in ten minutes and the whole school was crowded in the porch because of the monsoon rain.

qa.q: What did Harish feel when Mr Desai appeared?
qa.a: Relief and embarrassment together. His knees almost gave way and he flushed hot because everyone had seen.

qa.q: What did Harish do that helped?
qa.a: He accepted the teacher's help and shared the dates he remembered, rather than denying it out of fear.

qa.q: How might Ojas be seeing the moment?
qa.a: Probably caught and defensive, since the teacher called him away while the school watched. What drives him is not shown.

grounding: A teacher notices bullying and steps in; Harish feels relieved and embarrassed and gives details instead of denying it.
